title: Graphs and dynamic programming
summary: Traverse graphs with an explicit queue and visited set, then reuse subproblems instead of recomputing them.

scenario.briefing: The campus map service computed routes between buildings. A path search used pop on its work list and never marked visited nodes, so it returned long routes and looped on cycles. The planner also repeated the same subproblems when counting routes. Implement breadth-first search and review the repeated-work recurrence.

objectives.description: Apply the taught syntax in a working file.
Review an artifact and identify the concrete risks.

hints: Start the visited set with the start node and process the queue with a head index.
Mark a neighbor visited before you enqueue it; otherwise cycles enqueue it repeatedly.
Store the parent only on the first visit so the path stays shortest.
For the recurrence in the review, cache results by step count or fill a table from the base cases.

misconceptions.description: Using a stack when the problem needs breadth-first order.
misconceptions.testDescription: The search marks the start and processes the queue from its head.
misconceptions.feedback: A stack changes traversal to depth-first. Breadth-first shortest paths need a queue.

misconceptions.description: Marking nodes when they are removed instead of enqueued.
misconceptions.testDescription: A neighbor is marked before it can be enqueued twice.
misconceptions.feedback: Late marking lets the same node enter the frontier many times. Mark it when enqueued.
The recursive route count recomputes the same subproblems. Memoize or use bottom-up dynamic programming.

misconceptions.description: Assuming a plausible greedy rule is always optimal.
misconceptions.feedback: A greedy rule needs a proof or a counterexample check. The artifact's rule has neither.

sections.title: Breadth-first search explores by distance
sections.body: A queue processes nodes in the order they were discovered. Unweighted edges all cost one, so the first time BFS reaches a node is along a shortest path. Level order is the invariant that makes that true.

sections.title: Visited belongs at discovery
sections.body: A visited set stops cycles and duplicate work. Mark a node when it is enqueued, not when it is dequeued, or the same node can enter the queue many times. The parent map stores one predecessor per node and is written only on the first visit.

sections.title: A stack changes the question
sections.body: A stack, or recursion, follows one branch to the end. It answers reachability and structure questions, but the first path it finds is not generally shortest. Using pop on a BFS queue silently turns the search into depth-first search.

sections.title: Dynamic programming reuses overlapping subproblems
sections.body: A recurrence has overlapping subproblems when the same state appears through different branches. Memoization stores each state's result; bottom-up tables fill states in dependency order. Without reuse, the call tree can grow exponentially even when the number of distinct states is small.

sections.title: Greedy needs a proof
sections.body: A greedy algorithm commits to a locally best choice and never reconsiders. It is correct only when the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure hold. Coin change with denominations 1, 3, and 4 is a counterexample: greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 for 6, while 3 + 3 uses fewer coins.

vocabulary.definition: A traversal that visits nodes in order of their distance from the start.
A set of nodes already discovered, used to stop cycles and duplicate work.
A map from each discovered node to the node it was reached from.
Caching a function result by its arguments so each subproblem is solved once.
A recurrence that reaches the same state through multiple branches.
A strategy that commits to the locally best choice without revisiting it.

steps.title: Breadth-first shortest path
steps.prompt: Edit graphs.ts. Process the queue from its head, mark the start as visited, skip neighbors that are already visited, record each parent once, and rebuild the path from the goal.

tests.description: The search marks the start and processes the queue from its head.
A neighbor is marked before it can be enqueued twice.
A reachable goal returns a rebuilt path and an unreachable goal returns null.
The frontier no longer uses a stack pop or an array shift.

hints: Choose the frontier structure that matches breadth-first order.
Mark a node when it enters the frontier, not when it leaves.
Reconstruct the path by following parent links from the goal.
Use a queue, mark before enqueue, and return null when the frontier empties.

localVerification.description: Runs the repository content validator, which executes the same structural checks against the authored file.

steps.title: Review the repeated-work recurrence
steps.prompt: Review the artifact and select every real problem.

artifact.title: routes.ts
artifact.caption: The recurrence is correct, but each call recomputes the same step counts.

findings.label: countRoutes(steps - 2) is computed directly and again inside countRoutes(steps - 1).
The number of calls grows exponentially because no result is stored.
A memo table keyed by steps, or a bottom-up table, would reduce the work to linear time.
Choosing the two-step move whenever possible is optimal for every input.
The function is incorrect because it has no base case.

verdicts.label: Block the change until the repeated subproblems are cached.
The code only needs formatting changes.
Ship it; the recurrence is correct, so the cost is acceptable.

steps.explanation: The recurrence describes the correct number of routes, but it solves the same step counts repeatedly. The call tree doubles at each level, so countRoutes(30) performs an exponential amount of work. Cache each step count or fill a table from the base cases.
hints: Find overlapping subproblems that a cache would reuse.
Check whether the greedy choice is justified or only plausible.
Identify the base cases that stop the recursion.
Block the change: memoization is missing, the greedy rule is unproven, and a base case is wrong.
